items.title: 1.6.2 Operations on Complex Numbers in Polar Form

source_refs.note: Book pp. 16-18: printed heading "1.3.3 Operations on Complex Numbers in Polar Form" (out of sequence), addition/subtraction, multiplication (Example 13), division (Example 14), then Examples 15 and 16

blocks.text: 1.3.3 Operations on Complex Numbers in Polar Form

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints this heading as 1.3.3, which is out of sequence: it comes after 1.4.1 and continues the polar-form work. We keep the printed number so you can find it in your textbook; only the numbering is wrong.
Addition and Subtraction of Complex number in Polar form

Let \(z_1 = r_1(\cos\theta_1 + i\sin\theta_1)\) and \(z_2 = r_2(\cos\theta_2 + i\sin\theta_2)\) be two complex numbers in polar form. Their sum and difference can be written simply as
\[z_1 + z_2 = r_1(\cos\theta_1 + i\sin\theta_1)\]
\[\qquad + r_2(\cos\theta_2 + i\sin\theta_2)\]
\[z_1 - z_2 = r_1(\cos\theta_1 + i\sin\theta_1)\]
\[\qquad - r_2(\cos\theta_2 + i\sin\theta_2)\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
There is no shortcut for adding in polar form. Do not add the moduli and the angles. To get a single complex number, go back to rectangular form and collect real and imaginary parts:
\[z_1 + z_2 = (r_1\cos\theta_1 + r_2\cos\theta_2)\]
\[\qquad + i(r_1\sin\theta_1 + r_2\sin\theta_2)\]
Then, if needed, convert the answer to polar form again.
Why the shortcut fails: \(1(\cos 0 + i\sin 0) = 1\) and \(1(\cos\pi + i\sin\pi) = -1\) add to \(0\), not to \(2(\cos\pi + i\sin\pi) = -2\).
Multiplication of Complex number in Polar form

Let \(z_1 = r_1(\cos\theta_1 + i\sin\theta_1)\) and \(z_2 = r_2(\cos\theta_2 + i\sin\theta_2)\) be two complex numbers in polar form. The product can be derived by multiplying them directly and simplifying:
\[z_1 z_2 = r_1(\cos\theta_1 + i\sin\theta_1)\]
\[\qquad \times r_2(\cos\theta_2 + i\sin\theta_2)\]
Open the brackets (four products):
\[\cos\theta_1\cos\theta_2 + i\cos\theta_1\sin\theta_2\]
\[+\ i\sin\theta_1\cos\theta_2 + i^2\sin\theta_1\sin\theta_2\]
Use \(i^2 = -1\) and collect the real and imaginary parts:
\[(\cos\theta_1\cos\theta_2 - \sin\theta_1\sin\theta_2)\]
\[+\ i(\cos\theta_1\sin\theta_2 + \sin\theta_1\cos\theta_2)\]
Using the trigonometric identities (see Remember below):
\[z_1 z_2 = r_1 r_2[\cos(\theta_1 + \theta_2)\]
\[\qquad + i\sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2)]\]

blocks.text_alt: z one times z two equals r one r two times open bracket cos of theta one plus theta two plus i sin of theta one plus theta two close bracket

blocks.text: Thus, multiplying two complex numbers in polar form means multiplying their moduli and adding their arguments, i.e. \(\arg(z_1 z_2) = \arg(z_1) + \arg(z_2)\).

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text:
The two identities used above:
\[\cos(A + B) = \cos A\cos B - \sin A\sin B\]
\[\sin(A + B) = \sin A\cos B + \cos A\sin B\]
The real part of the product matched the first one, and the imaginary part matched the second one.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Picture it: multiplying by \(z_2\) stretches \(z_1\) by the factor \(r_2\) and turns it through the angle \(\theta_2\).
The rule \(\arg(z_1 z_2) = \arg z_1 + \arg z_2\) is true up to a multiple of \(2\pi\). If you need the principal argument, add or subtract \(2\pi\) to bring the sum into \((-\pi, \pi]\).

blocks.title: Example 13
blocks.problem: Find the product of \(5\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{6} + i\sin\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\) and \(4\left(\cos\frac{3\pi}{2} + i\sin\frac{3\pi}{2}\right)\).
steps:
Given: \(z_1 = 5\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{6} + i\sin\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\) and \(z_2 = 4\left(\cos\frac{3\pi}{2} + i\sin\frac{3\pi}{2}\right)\).
To find: \(z_1 z_2\).
Method: both numbers are already in polar form, so use the product formula: multiply the moduli, add the arguments.

Read off r and θ
\[r_1 = 5,\quad \theta_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\]
\[r_2 = 4,\quad \theta_2 = \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\]
Why: compare each number with \(r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)\).

Substitute in the product formula
\[z_1 z_2 = r_1 r_2[\cos(\theta_1 + \theta_2)\]
\[\qquad + i\sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2)]\]
with
\[r_1 r_2 = 5 \times 4\]
\[\theta_1 + \theta_2 = \dfrac{\pi}{6} + \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\]
Why: this is exactly the formula derived above.

Simplify the modulus and the angle
\[5 \times 4 = 20\]
\[\dfrac{\pi}{6} + \dfrac{3\pi}{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{6} + \dfrac{9\pi}{6}\]
\[= \dfrac{10\pi}{6} = \dfrac{5\pi}{3}\]
So
\[z_1 z_2 = 20\left(\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{3} + i\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\right)\]
Why: to add fractions, write them with the common denominator 6.

Check (multiply in rectangular form)
\[z_1 = 5\left(\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \tfrac{1}{2}i\right)\]
\[z_2 = 4(0 - i) = -4i\]
\[z_1 z_2 = -4i \cdot \left(\tfrac{5\sqrt{3}}{2} + \tfrac{5}{2}i\right)\]
\[= -10\sqrt{3}\,i - 10i^2\]
\[= 10 - 10\sqrt{3}\,i\]
And \(20\left(\cos\frac{5\pi}{3} + i\sin\frac{5\pi}{3}\right) = 20\left(\tfrac{1}{2} - \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i\right) = 10 - 10\sqrt{3}\,i\). Both agree.
Note: \(5\pi/3\) is not in \((-\pi, \pi]\); the principal argument of the product is \(5\pi/3 - 2\pi = -\pi/3\), so the same answer is \(20\left(\cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{3}\right) + i\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\right)\).

blocks.text: Division of Complex Number in Polar Form

Let \(z_1 = r_1(\cos\theta_1 + i\sin\theta_1)\) and \(z_2 = r_2(\cos\theta_2 + i\sin\theta_2)\) be two complex numbers in polar form. The formula for dividing them can be derived by rationalizing the denominator (\(z_2 \ne 0\), so \(r_2 \ne 0\)):
\[\dfrac{z_1}{z_2} = \dfrac{r_1(\cos\theta_1 + i\sin\theta_1)}{r_2(\cos\theta_2 + i\sin\theta_2)}\]
Multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of \(\cos\theta_2 + i\sin\theta_2\), which is \(\cos\theta_2 - i\sin\theta_2\). Work out each part separately.
Denominator:
\[\cos^2\theta_2 - i^2\sin^2\theta_2\]
\[= \cos^2\theta_2 + \sin^2\theta_2 = 1\]
Numerator:
\[\cos\theta_1\cos\theta_2 - i\cos\theta_1\sin\theta_2\]
\[+\ i\sin\theta_1\cos\theta_2 - i^2\sin\theta_1\sin\theta_2\]
\[= (\cos\theta_1\cos\theta_2 + \sin\theta_1\sin\theta_2)\]
\[\ + i(\sin\theta_1\cos\theta_2 - \cos\theta_1\sin\theta_2)\]
Using the trigonometric identities (see Remember below):
\[\dfrac{z_1}{z_2} = \dfrac{r_1}{r_2}[\cos(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\]
\[\qquad + i\sin(\theta_1 - \theta_2)]\]

blocks.text_alt: z one over z two equals r one over r two times open bracket cos of theta one minus theta two plus i sin of theta one minus theta two close bracket

blocks.text: Thus, when dividing two complex numbers, the modulus of the result is the quotient of their moduli, and the argument of the result is the difference between their arguments, i.e. \(\arg\left(\frac{z_1}{z_2}\right) = \arg(z_1) - \arg(z_2)\).

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text:
The identities used for division:
\[\cos(A - B) = \cos A\cos B + \sin A\sin B\]
\[\sin(A - B) = \sin A\cos B - \cos A\sin B\]
And the denominator became 1 because \(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1\).

blocks.title: Example 14
steps:
Given: \(z_1 = \frac{2}{7}\left(\cos\frac{7\pi}{6} + i\sin\frac{7\pi}{6}\right)\), \(z_2 = \frac{3}{5}\left(\cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right) + i\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\right)\).
To find: \(\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}\).
Method: both are in polar form, so use the quotient formula: divide the moduli, subtract the arguments.

Read off r and θ
\[r_1 = \dfrac{2}{7},\quad \theta_1 = \dfrac{7\pi}{6}\]
\[r_2 = \dfrac{3}{5},\quad \theta_2 = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}\]
Why: compare each number with \(r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)\). Keep the minus sign of \(\theta_2\).

Substitute in the quotient formula
\[\dfrac{z_1}{z_2} = \dfrac{r_1}{r_2}[\cos(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\]
\[\qquad + i\sin(\theta_1 - \theta_2)]\]
with
\[\dfrac{r_1}{r_2} = \dfrac{2}{7} \times \dfrac{5}{3}\]
\[\theta_1 - \theta_2 = \dfrac{7\pi}{6} - \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\]
Why: dividing by \(\frac{3}{5}\) is multiplying by \(\frac{5}{3}\).

Simplify the modulus and the angle
\[\dfrac{2}{7} \times \dfrac{5}{3} = \dfrac{10}{21}\]
\[\dfrac{7\pi}{6} + \dfrac{\pi}{2} = \dfrac{7\pi}{6} + \dfrac{3\pi}{6}\]
\[= \dfrac{10\pi}{6} = \dfrac{5\pi}{3}\]
So
\[\dfrac{z_1}{z_2} = \dfrac{10}{21}\left(\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{3} + i\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\right)\]
Why: subtracting a negative angle means adding it: \(-(-\pi/2) = +\pi/2\).

Check (divide in rectangular form)
\[z_1 = \tfrac{2}{7}\left(-\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - \tfrac{1}{2}i\right) = -\tfrac{\sqrt{3} + i}{7}\]
\[z_2 = \tfrac{3}{5}(0 - i) = -\tfrac{3}{5}i\]
\[\dfrac{z_1}{z_2} = \dfrac{5(\sqrt{3} + i)}{21i}\]
\[= \dfrac{5(\sqrt{3} + i)(-i)}{21}\]
\[= \dfrac{5}{21} - \dfrac{5\sqrt{3}}{21}i\]
And \(\frac{10}{21}\left(\tfrac{1}{2} - \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i\right) = \frac{5}{21} - \frac{5\sqrt{3}}{21}i\). Both agree, so the book's answer is correct. (Principal argument: \(5\pi/3 - 2\pi = -\pi/3\).)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The book prints Examples 15 and 16 here. They do not use the polar formulas; they practise the modulus, the conjugate and the argument with \(z = x + iy\), and lead to the equation of a line and of a circle.

blocks.title: Example 15
blocks.problem: If \(z = x + iy\), then write the equation \(|3z - i| = |3\overline{z} + 7|\) in terms of \(x\) and \(y\).
steps:
Given: \(|3z - i| = |3\overline{z} + 7|\) ... (i), with \(z = x + iy\).
To find: the same equation using only \(x\) and \(y\).
Method: write each side as \(a + ib\), use \(|a + ib| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\), then square and simplify.

Left side
\[3z - i = 3(x + iy) - i\]
\[= 3x + i(3y - 1)\]
\[|3z - i| = \sqrt{(3x)^2 + (3y - 1)^2}\]
Why: collect the real part \(3x\) and the imaginary part \(3y - 1\) before taking the modulus.

Right side
\[\overline{z} = x - iy\]
\[3\overline{z} + 7 = 3x - 3iy + 7\]
\[= (3x + 7) + i(-3y)\]
\[|3\overline{z} + 7| = \sqrt{(3x + 7)^2 + (-3y)^2}\]
Why: the conjugate changes the sign of the imaginary part.

Substitute in (i) and square both sides
\[\sqrt{(3x)^2 + (3y - 1)^2} = \sqrt{(3x + 7)^2 + (-3y)^2}\]
\[(3x)^2 + (3y - 1)^2 = (3x + 7)^2 + (-3y)^2\]
Why: squaring removes the square roots; both sides are non-negative, so nothing is lost.

Expand and simplify
\[9x^2 + 9y^2 - 6y + 1\]
\[= 9x^2 + 42x + 49 + 9y^2\]
\[-6y + 1 = 42x + 49\]
\[-6y = 42x + 48\]
\[y = -7x - 8\]
Why: \(9x^2\) and \(9y^2\) cancel from both sides; then divide by \(-6\).

Check
Take \(x = -1\): then \(y = -7(-1) - 8 = -1\), so \(z = -1 - i\).
\[3z - i = -3 - 4i,\quad |{-3} - 4i| = 5\]
\[3\overline{z} + 7 = 4 + 3i,\quad |4 + 3i| = 5\]
Both sides are equal, as expected. The equation \(y = -7x - 8\) represents a straight line in the complex plane.

blocks.title: Example 16
blocks.problem: Show that \((x + 2)^2 + y^2 = 8\) if \(\arg\left(\frac{z + 2i}{z - 2i}\right) = \frac{3\pi}{4}\) for \(z = x + iy\).
steps:
Given: \(z = x + iy\) and \(\arg\left(\frac{z + 2i}{z - 2i}\right) = \frac{3\pi}{4}\).
To prove: \((x + 2)^2 + y^2 = 8\).
Method: write the fraction in the form \(a + ib\) (multiply by the conjugate of the denominator), then use \(\tan(\arg) = \dfrac{\text{imaginary part}}{\text{real part}}\).

Substitute z
\[\dfrac{z + 2i}{z - 2i} = \dfrac{x + iy + 2i}{x + iy - 2i}\]
\[= \dfrac{x + i(y + 2)}{x + i(y - 2)}\]
Why: group the imaginary terms together.

Multiply by the conjugate of the denominator
\[= \dfrac{x + i(y + 2)}{x + i(y - 2)} \times \dfrac{x - i(y - 2)}{x - i(y - 2)}\]
Numerator:
\[x^2 - ix(y - 2) + ix(y + 2)\]
\[\ - i^2(y + 2)(y - 2)\]
\[= (x^2 + y^2 - 4) + 4ix\]
Denominator:
\[x^2 + (y - 2)^2\]
Why: \((a + ib)(a - ib) = a^2 + b^2\) is real, so the fraction separates into real and imaginary parts. Here \(-i^2 = +1\) and \((y + 2)(y - 2) = y^2 - 4\).

Separate the parts
\[\dfrac{z + 2i}{z - 2i} = \dfrac{x^2 + y^2 - 4}{x^2 + (y - 2)^2} + i\,\dfrac{4x}{x^2 + (y - 2)^2}\]
Why: now the real part and the imaginary part are clear.

Use the argument
\[\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\text{Im}}{\text{Re}}\right) = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}\]
The common denominator \(x^2 + (y - 2)^2\) cancels:
\[\dfrac{4x}{x^2 + y^2 - 4} = \tan\dfrac{3\pi}{4} = -1\]
Why: for an argument \(\theta\), \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{imaginary part}}{\text{real part}}\), and \(\tan\frac{3\pi}{4} = -1\).

Simplify and complete the square
\[4x = -1(x^2 + y^2 - 4)\]
\[x^2 + 4x + y^2 = 4\]
Add 4 to both sides:
\[x^2 + 4x + 4 + y^2 = 8\]
\[(x + 2)^2 + y^2 = 8\]
Why: \(x^2 + 4x + 4 = (x + 2)^2\); half of the coefficient 4 is 2, and \(2^2 = 4\).

Check
Take a point of this circle with \(x > 0\): \(x = \tfrac{1}{2}\), \(y = \tfrac{\sqrt{7}}{2}\) (then \((2.5)^2 + 1.75 = 8\)). For it, \(x^2 + y^2 - 4 = -2 < 0\) and \(4x = 2 > 0\), so \(\frac{z + 2i}{z - 2i}\) lies in the second quadrant with \(\tan = 2/(-2) = -1\): its argument is \(\frac{3\pi}{4}\). Correct.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A careful point about Example 16 (it links to the Principal Argument rule). \(\tan\theta = -1\) is true for \(\theta = \frac{3\pi}{4}\) and also for \(\theta = -\frac{\pi}{4}\). The argument is \(\frac{3\pi}{4}\) (second quadrant) only when the real part is negative and the imaginary part positive, i.e. \(4x > 0\), so \(x > 0\).
So every \(z\) with this argument lies on the circle \((x + 2)^2 + y^2 = 8\), which is what the example asks us to show. But not every point of the circle works: for \(x = -1\), \(y = \sqrt{7}\) the argument is \(-\frac{\pi}{4}\). The exact locus is the part of the circle with \(x > 0\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
• Addition and subtraction: no polar shortcut; add the real parts and the imaginary parts.
• Multiplication: multiply the moduli, add the arguments: \(z_1 z_2 = r_1 r_2\operatorname{cis}(\theta_1 + \theta_2)\).
• Division: divide the moduli, subtract the arguments: \(\dfrac{z_1}{z_2} = \dfrac{r_1}{r_2}\operatorname{cis}(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\), \(z_2 \ne 0\).
• Adjust a result angle by \(\pm 2\pi\) if the principal argument is needed.
• For \(|\ldots| = |\ldots|\) equations: write each side as \(a + ib\), take moduli, square.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
• Adding moduli and angles when adding complex numbers. That rule is only for multiplication (with multiplied moduli).
• Dividing the angles or multiplying the angles. Angles are added (product) or subtracted (quotient).
• Losing the minus sign: \(\theta_1 - \theta_2\) with \(\theta_2 = -\pi/2\) becomes \(\theta_1 + \pi/2\).
• In Example 15, forgetting that \(\overline{z} = x - iy\) changes the sign of \(y\).
• In Example 16, using \(\tan\theta = -1\) without checking the quadrant of the argument.
